name: Buddha Park (Tathagata Tsal)

local_name.name: Tathagata Tsal
local_name.meaning: grove (park) of the Tathagata, an epithet of the Buddha

tagline: A 130 ft copper Buddha with Mount Narsing behind it
meta_description: Buddha Park (Tathagata Tsal), Ravangla: the 130 ft Buddha, its 2013 consecration, museum, entry fee, timings, how to reach and when to go.
summary: Buddha Park, or Tathagata Tsal, is a landscaped pilgrimage park above Ravangla at about 2,115 m. Its centrepiece is a 130 ft (40 m) statue of the Buddha clad in about 60 tonnes of copper, built from 2006 to 2013 for the 2550th Buddha Jayanti and consecrated by the 14th Dalai Lama on 25 March 2013.
intro: Tathagata Tsal sits on the slope just above Ravangla market, within the wider religious grounds of the old Rabong monastery. A long, formal avenue leads from the gate past gardens and a small lake, Cho Djo, to a broad platform where the Buddha sits in meditation, gold-toned and serene, with the forested ridge of Mount Narsing and, on clear days, the Kangchenjunga range behind.

The statue was raised to mark the 2550th anniversary of the Buddha's birth, celebrated across the Buddhist world in 2006–07. Work began in 2006 and the 14th Dalai Lama consecrated it on 25 March 2013. The copper was shaped by repoussé, hammered from behind, the traditional Himalayan technique for large images. Inside the base is a museum with a spiral gallery on the Buddha's life.

The park is one of the most visited places in South Sikkim, so timing matters. Come at opening time on a clear October to February morning for the mountain backdrop and quiet paths. Allow 1.5–2 hours: walk the avenue, circle the statue, visit the museum and sit by the lake. Then drive 6 km on to Ralang Monastery.

story.title: Why a 130 ft Buddha came to Ravangla
story.text: In 2006, Buddhist countries and communities marked the Buddha Jayanti, 2,550 years since the birth of the Buddha by the traditional reckoning. The Government of Sikkim chose to commemorate it with a statue, and picked a site at Ravangla within the larger religious complex of Rabong monastery, long a place of pilgrimage in the south. Ralang, one of Sikkim's important Kagyu monasteries, is just 6 km away, and the slopes look out to Mount Narsing. Work ran from 2006 to 2013. The statue was made using repoussé, where sheets of metal are hammered from the reverse side into shape, using about 60 tonnes of copper over an internal frame. On 25 March 2013 the 14th Dalai Lama consecrated it. Around the statue the planners added a meditation centre, a Buddhist conclave hall, the small Cho Djo lake and a museum whose spiral gallery tells the Buddha's life. Together with Samdruptse and Char Dham near Namchi, it made the district a pilgrimage circuit in its own right.

little_known.fact: The statue is clad in about 60 tonnes of copper shaped by repoussé, hammering the metal from behind, the traditional method for large Himalayan sacred images.
The park was built within the larger religious complex of Rabong monastery, already a centuries-old place of pilgrimage before the statue was planned.
A museum inside the statue's base has a spiral gallery; walking it upward takes you through the Buddha's life in sequence.

facts: 130 ft Buddha, museum, Mount Narsing backdrop

highlights.title: The 130 ft Buddha
highlights.text: Seated in meditation, about 40 m tall and clad in copper, consecrated in 2013. Walk around the base clockwise. Morning light is usually the most even for photographs.

highlights.title: Museum and spiral gallery
highlights.text: Inside the base, a museum whose gallery spirals upward through the Buddha's life, with paintings and texts. Allow 30 minutes. Photography inside may be restricted; ask at the door.

highlights.title: Mount Narsing backdrop
highlights.text: On clear days the snow peaks rise behind the statue, a view that shows up on half of Sikkim's postcards. October to February mornings give the best chance.

highlights.title: Cho Djo lake and gardens
highlights.text: A small lake surrounded by forest and landscaped paths, with benches and flowers. A quiet spot to sit away from the main platform, especially in late afternoon.

highlights.title: Rabong monastery grounds
highlights.text: The park lies within the wider religious complex of Rabong monastery. Look for older chortens and shrines on the slope, a reminder that the site was sacred before the statue.

how_to_reach.text: Take a shared jeep to Ravangla from Gangtok (about ₹250–400, 3 hours) or Namchi (₹100–150, 1 hour). From Ravangla market the park gate is about 1.5 km uphill: a 20–25 minute walk or a short taxi ride for ₹100–200.

Most visitors include Buddha Park in a Ravangla day with Ralang Monastery and sometimes Borong or Temi, about ₹2,500–3,500 for a small car. A day trip from Gangtok covering Buddha Park and Ralang costs roughly ₹4,500–6,000.

About 120–125 km and 4.5–5 hours by car via Melli and Namchi or via Singtam. Sleep in Ravangla to visit at opening time. If NH10 is closed after monsoon slides, the route through Darjeeling district and Jorethang is the usual alternative.

where_to_stay: Stay in Ravangla, 5–10 minutes away. Several budget hotels line the road up to the park, with doubles from about ₹1,500–2,500, some with direct statue views. Mt. Narsing Village Resort on the Pelling road offers garden cottages at value prices, and The Barfung Retreat in Barfung village is our quiet comfort choice. Kewzing homestays and Bon Farmhouse are 20 minutes downhill.
tips: Arrive at opening time (around 9 am) for clear views and quiet paths.
Walk around the statue clockwise and remove shoes where signs ask.
Bring a warm layer; the open platform at 2,115 m can be windy.
Allow 30 minutes for the museum inside the base.
Pair with Ralang Monastery, 6 km away, in the same morning.

experiences.title: Buddha Park at opening time
experiences.image_query: Tathagata Tsal Ravangla Buddha statue Narsing
experiences.summary: Be at the gate when Tathagata Tsal opens, walk the long avenue while it is still quiet, circle the 130 ft Buddha clockwise, visit the museum and sit by the lake. The mountain backdrop is clearest in the first hours.
body: The park has generally opened around 9 am. Arrive a few minutes early, buy your ticket and walk the formal avenue towards the statue without crowds. On a clear morning the Buddha sits against a backdrop of forested ridges with snow peaks rising behind, the classic view of Ravangla.

Circle the statue clockwise on the platform, as pilgrims do. Monks and local families often light butter lamps or offer prayers; join quietly or watch from a distance. Then enter the museum in the base, where a spiral gallery takes you through the Buddha's life from birth to parinirvana.

Finish at Cho Djo lake, a small pond ringed by forest, or on a bench in the gardens. By 11 am tour groups from Gangtok and Pelling arrive and the paths fill. Allow two hours in total and continue to Ralang Monastery, 6 km away, before lunch.

faqs.q: What are Buddha Park's opening hours?
faqs.a: The park has generally been open from about 9 am to 6 pm daily, though hours can change by season. Check with your hotel the evening before. Mornings are best for both light and crowds.

faqs.q: How long does it take to see Buddha Park?
faqs.a: Allow 1.5–2 hours: about 20 minutes for the avenue, 20 minutes around the statue, 30 minutes in the museum and some time in the gardens. Photographers and pilgrims may want longer.

faqs.q: Is Buddha Park suitable for wheelchair users?
faqs.a: Mostly. The main avenue is broad and paved with gentle slopes, and the platform around the statue is level. Some areas involve steps. The museum interior may be harder to access. Ask at the gate for the easiest route.

experiences.title: The Buddha's life in the spiral museum
experiences.summary: Inside the statue's base, a museum's spiral gallery tells the Buddha's life in sequence, from birth at Lumbini to enlightenment and final passing. A clear introduction for children and first-time visitors to Buddhism before you visit Sikkim's monasteries.
body: Many visitors walk straight past the entrance in the statue's base, which is a pity. Inside, the museum's gallery winds upward in a spiral, and the walls tell the story of the Buddha's life step by step: his birth as Prince Siddhartha, the four sights, renunciation, enlightenment under the bodhi tree, the first sermon and the final passing.

For children and first-time visitors it is the best primer for everything else they will see in Sikkim. Once you know the story, the paintings in Ralang, Pemayangtse or Rumtek suddenly make sense: you recognise the scenes, the gestures of the hands, the symbols carried by each figure.

Allow 30–45 minutes. Photography rules inside can be strict, so ask at the entrance. Walk slowly and in silence when monks or pilgrims are present. Shoes may need to be removed. The museum is included with the park ticket at the time of writing.

faqs.q: Is there a separate fee for the Buddha Park museum?
faqs.a: At the time of writing the museum is included with the park entry ticket. Rules can change, so check at the gate. Some special exhibitions or audio guides, if offered, may carry a small extra charge.

faqs.q: Can we take photos inside the museum?
faqs.a: Photography may be restricted inside the museum to protect the paintings and respect the sacred setting. Ask staff at the entrance. Outside, around the statue and gardens, photography is generally allowed.

faqs.q: Is the museum interesting for children?
faqs.a: Yes. The spiral gallery tells the Buddha's life as a story in pictures, which most children follow easily. Ask them to spot the elephant, the bodhi tree and the deer park as you walk. It makes later monastery visits far more interesting for them.

experiences.title: Butter lamps and dusk at Tathagata Tsal
experiences.summary: Return late in the afternoon, when the tour groups have left, to light a butter lamp, walk a last kora around the statue and watch the copper Buddha turn gold in the low sun. Quiet and reflective, and very different from the midday bustle.
body: Butter lamps are a central offering in Tibetan Buddhism, lit to dispel darkness and ignorance and to dedicate merit to others. At Buddha Park, lamps are offered in a dedicated lamp house or at shrines near the statue. A small donation covers the cost of a lamp; staff or monks will show you where to light it.

Come in the hour before closing, roughly 4–6 pm depending on the season. The light turns warm and low, the statue's copper skin glows, and the paths are almost empty. Walk a slow kora around the base, then sit by Cho Djo lake as the forest goes quiet.

Check closing time when you buy your ticket, as the gate may shut before full sunset in winter. Dress warmly: Ravangla cools fast after 4 pm. This pairs well with a morning at Ralang or Temi, leaving the afternoon for Buddha Park.

faqs.q: Can non-Buddhists light butter lamps?
faqs.a: Yes. Lighting a butter lamp is open to anyone who does it respectfully. You can make a wish or dedicate it to someone. Follow staff guidance on where and how to light it, and leave a small donation.

faqs.q: What time does Buddha Park close?
faqs.a: It has generally closed around 6 pm, earlier in some winter months. Ask at the gate when you enter. In December and January, sunset is around 4:50–5 pm, so the late-afternoon light comes before closing.

faqs.q: Is the evening visit worth a second ticket?
faqs.a: If you enjoy quiet places, yes. A second visit costs only the entry fee, about ₹50 for Indians. If time is short, a single visit at opening time gives the best views; late afternoon gives the best atmosphere.

experiences.title: Walk from Buddha Park towards Ralang
experiences.summary: After your visit, walk downhill from Buddha Park along the quiet road towards Ralang Monastery, about 6 km, through village fields and forest with views of Narsing and the Rangeet valley. Send your car ahead to meet you at Ralang.
body: Ralang Monastery is about 6 km from Ravangla by road. Instead of driving, walk it: the road descends gently through Bhutia and Nepali villages, cardamom groves and patches of forest, with long views across the Rangeet valley to the hills of West Sikkim and, on clear days, the snow peaks above.

Traffic is light outside festival days. Stop to watch farmers in the fields, children on their way home from school, and prayer flags snapping in the wind on the ridges. The walk takes 2–2.5 hours at an easy pace, losing a few hundred metres of height.

Arrange for your driver to meet you at Ralang's new monastery, Palchen Choeling. Visit the monastery, then ask the driver to take you to the old Ralang monastery nearby. Carry water and a snack; there are a few small shops on the way.

faqs.q: How far is Ralang from Buddha Park?
faqs.a: About 6 km by road, roughly 15 minutes by car or 2–2.5 hours on foot downhill. The walk follows the motor road, which is quiet on most days. Watch for vehicles on bends and keep to the edge.

faqs.q: Is the walk to Ralang suitable for children?
faqs.a: Yes, for children used to walking. It is mostly gentle downhill on a road, with no technical sections. Keep children on the inside of bends and take breaks. You can always call the car if anyone tires.

faqs.q: Can we walk back uphill to Ravangla?
faqs.a: You can, but it is a steady 2.5–3 hour climb. Most people walk down and drive back. If you prefer the uphill for exercise, start from Ralang in the morning when it is cool.

faqs.q: How tall is the Buddha statue at Ravangla?
faqs.a: The statue is 130 ft, about 40 m, tall and clad in around 60 tonnes of copper. It was built between 2006 and 2013 to mark the 2550th anniversary of the Buddha's birth, and consecrated by the 14th Dalai Lama on 25 March 2013.

faqs.q: What is the entry fee for Buddha Park Ravangla?
faqs.a: Entry has been about ₹50 for Indian visitors and ₹100 for foreign nationals, with parking extra. Fees can be revised, so check current status before you travel. The museum inside the statue base is included at the time of writing.

faqs.q: What are Buddha Park's timings?
faqs.a: The park has generally been open from around 9 am to 6 pm every day. Timings can vary by season and on special occasions. Visit early for clear views of Mount Narsing and fewer crowds.

faqs.q: How far is Buddha Park from Gangtok?
faqs.a: About 66 km and 3 hours by road to Ravangla, plus a few minutes up to the park. A day trip from Gangtok is possible but long; better to stay a night in Ravangla and visit Ralang Monastery as well.

faqs.q: Why is it called Tathagata Tsal?
faqs.a: Tathagata is a title of the Buddha, often translated as the thus-gone one, and tsal means a garden or grove in Tibetan. So Tathagata Tsal means the Buddha's garden or park. Locally it is simply called Buddha Park.

faqs.q: When is the best time to visit Buddha Park?
faqs.a: October to February mornings for clear skies and mountain views behind the statue. March to May is pleasant with flowers but hazier. June to September brings rain and cloud. Buddha Purnima (April–May) draws many pilgrims.

faqs.q: Can we see snow peaks from Buddha Park?
faqs.a: On clear days, yes. The Narsing range and other peaks of the Kangchenjunga massif appear behind the statue, best from October to February in the morning. In the monsoon and spring haze, mountain views are often hidden.

faqs.q: Is Buddha Park good for families?
faqs.a: Very. Broad paved paths, gardens, a lake, a museum that tells a story, and clean toilets make it one of the easiest family sites in Sikkim. Children enjoy the scale of the statue. Bring warm layers, as it is breezy at 2,115 m.

faqs.q: What else is near Buddha Park?
faqs.a: Ralang Monastery (6 km), Borong village and hot spring (about 17 km), Kewzing's Bon monastery (about 10 km), the Maenam forest trek (starting above Ravangla) and Temi tea garden (about an hour away). Ravangla market is 1.5 km below.
